representations.text:
Your main change was a temporary HRV dip: RMSSD fell to 22–28 ms on April 3–6, compared with your 28-day baseline range of 43–47 ms. It returned to 43–47 ms on April 7 and stayed there through April 12. Those four days lowered the 14-day average to 39.4 from 44.5 ms (12%); this was not a sustained decline across the whole window.

Resting heart rate stayed within 55–57 bpm, including during the dip. Sleep averaged 7h49 versus 7h50, with starts around 22:42–22:58 and waking consistently at 07:00; weekday and weekend sleep were similar. Steps were unchanged at about 8,061 versus 8,054 daily. Active time eased to 53 from 55 minutes, particularly on weekends (51 versus 56), while low movement remained about 450 minutes daily.

Activity still began at 21:00, and its association with sleep ending the following morning was weak. No clear accompanying sleep or movement change explains the HRV dip. All metrics were available; tracking whether this brief pattern recurs could be useful.

Your recorded steps dropped sharply at the start of March 30–April 12 and remained lower throughout: 2,335 daily versus your 28-day baseline of 8,009, a reduction of 5,675 (71%). Every day was between 2,064 and 2,636 steps, below the baseline range of 7,607–8,342, with no return by the final day. Weekends averaged 2,477 and weekdays 2,278, so the reduction affected both.

Other measures stayed close to baseline: active time averaged 54.6 versus 55.1 minutes, still beginning at 21:00, and low movement averaged 453 versus 451 minutes. Weekend active time decreased to 52 from 57 minutes, while weekday time rose slightly to 56 from 54. These records do not show a comparable reduction in moving minutes.

Sleep remained about 7h50, starting around 22:42–22:57 and ending at 07:00. Resting heart rate averaged 56.0 versus 55.7 bpm; HRV averaged 45.3 versus 45.1 ms. Activity had only a modest inverse association with next-morning sleep duration. Coverage was complete. Checking whether the persistent step change matches your recorded movement could help clarify this discrepancy.

Your heart-rate and HRV changes occurred in separate four-day stretches. Resting heart rate rose to 65–67 bpm on April 3–6, versus your 28-day baseline range of 55–57, then returned to 55–57 on April 7 through the end. HRV stayed at 44–47 ms during that rise, then fell to 23–26 ms on April 7–10, versus its baseline range of 43–47. It returned to 45 ms on April 11–12.

These local changes raised the 14-day heart-rate average to 58.7 from 56.0 bpm and lowered HRV to 38.9 from 45.0 ms (13%). They were not simultaneous changes, and the lower weekday HRV average reflects the April 7–10 stretch rather than an established weekly pattern.

Sleep remained about 7h50, with slightly less variability, starts around 22:44–22:56 and consistent 07:00 waking. Steps stayed near 8,000 daily and active time near 55 minutes, beginning at 21:00; low movement decreased slightly to 447 from 451 minutes. Activity and next-morning sleep showed little association. All measurements were available. Further recording could show whether either brief change recurs.

Your steps shifted down from March 30 and remained lower through April 12: 6,433 daily versus your 28-day baseline of 9,552, a reduction of 3,119 (33%). All 13 recorded days were between 6,262 and 6,675 steps, below the baseline range of 9,307–9,793, with no return. Both weekdays and weekends showed the reduction; weekends remained slightly higher (6,500 versus 6,404).

April 7 had only 360 minutes of daytime wear, so steps, active time and low movement are missing, not zero. The other days had full daytime coverage. Active time decreased only slightly, to 53.5 from 55.1 minutes, with intervals still beginning at 21:00. Low movement averaged 451 versus 448 minutes. Daily steps and active minutes showed essentially no association within this window.

Sleep stayed about 7h50, with starts around 22:44–22:55 and waking at 07:00 across weekdays and weekends. Resting heart rate stayed near 56 bpm, and HRV near 45–46 ms with less variability. Activity had a modest inverse association with next-morning sleep duration across 12 pairs, without establishing causation. Continued complete daytime recording could help confirm the lower step pattern.
